A. Developing the Rate Year Revenue Forecast 
13 
Q. 
Please describe Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-2), Schedule 1. 
14 
A. 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-2), Schedule 1 shows the components of forecast 
15 
electric operating revenues for the Rate Year and Data Years 1 and 2.  
16 
Electric operating revenues include base delivery revenue, commodity 
17 
revenue, gross revenue tax revenue, and miscellaneous revenue.  
18 
Commodity revenue includes electric supply costs, legacy transition charge 
19 
(“LTC”), new hedge adjustment (“NHA”), and the New York Power 
20 
Authority 
(“NYPA”) 
Hydropower 
Benefit 
(“NYPA 
Hydro”).  
21 


--- Page 10 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 7 of 91 
Miscellaneous revenues include, but are not limited to, wholesale 
1 
transmission revenue, late payment charges, pole attachment revenue, rents 
2 
from electric properties, revenue from energy service companies 
3 
(“ESCOs”) participating in the Purchase of Receivables (“POR”) program, 
4 
and deferral recoveries. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
Did the Panel reflect any impacts to the revenue forecast from the 
7 
coronavirus pandemic (COVID-19)? 
8 
A. 
Other than the impacts to the Company’s sales forecast as explained in the 
9 
direct testimony of Company Witness Joseph E. Gredder, the Panel did not 
10 
reflect any discrete adjustments to capture potential impacts to the revenue 
11 
forecast, including miscellaneous revenue or tariff fees, resulting from 
12 
COVID-19.  For example, the forecast of late payment charges and re-
13 
establishment charges were based on the Historic Test Year levels.  At this 
14 
time, the Panel cannot project the potential COVID-19 impacts on these 
15 
types of charges in the Rate Year or Data Years, and assumed that any 
16 
impacts to these or any other components of the revenue forecast affected 
17 
by the timing of COVID-19 moratoriums (e.g., temporary suspension of 
18 
certain tariff fees) will be addressed in the Commission’s COVID-19 
19 
proceeding (Case 20-M-0266). 
20 
 
21

Q. 
How were the forecast billing determinants developed for the service 
14 
classes other than outdoor lighting? 
15 
A. 
The kWh billing determinants by voltage delivery level (“VDL”) for the 
16 
Rate Year were developed by applying historic percentages (twelve months 
17 
ended September 30, 2019) to forecast sales.  The kW billing determinants 
18 
were developed by applying a historic load factor ratio to the forecast kWh.  
19 
The historic load factor ratio is based on the twelve months ended 
20 
September 30, 2019 and is equal to historic demand divided by historic 
21 


--- Page 13 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel

kWh.  Similarly, the reactive kVA (“RkVA”) was forecast based on a 
1 
historic ratio for each VDL.  Schedules 1-3 of Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-2) 
2 
summarize the base delivery revenue, commodity revenue, and gross 
3 
revenue tax revenue by service classification for the Rate Year and Data 
4 
Years 1 and 2.  Those schedules also summarize the energy sales (kWh) and 
5 
billing demands (kW) used as billing determinants for rate design purposes.

2. Revenue Forecast for Customers with Special Contracts under 
3 
SC-12 
4 
 
5 
Q. 
How did the Company forecast revenues for SC-12?  
6 
A. 
Under SC-12, which pertains to special contract customers, qualifying 
7 
customers receive discounted service for all or part of their load and/or 
8 
receive first-through-the-meter billing for their NYPA allocation.  The 
9 
Company forecasts revenue from SC-12 customers at their otherwise 
10 
applicable standard tariff rates and includes that revenue with the otherwise 
11 
applicable (parent) service classification revenues.  As shown on Exhibit 
12 
___ (E-RDP-2), Schedule 1, there is no forecast discount for the Rate Year 
13 
for SC-12 because the Company currently has no SC-12 customers 
14 
receiving a discount from standard tariff rates.  The Company does have 
15 
customers with NYPA allocations receiving first-through-the-meter billing 
16 
methodology, which requires them to have an SC-12 contract. 
17 
 
18

Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 13 of 91 
C. Forecast of Commodity Revenues 
1 
Q. 
How did the Company forecast commodity revenues?   
2 
A. 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-2), Schedules 1-3 set forth the Company’s commodity 
3 
revenue forecast, which is based on the June 11, 2020 Intercontinental 
4 
Exchange (“ICE”) forward curve market prices.  Commodity revenues 
5 
include several elements.  First, commodity revenues include electricity 
6 
supply costs, which are calculated using forecast monthly load zone 
7 
weighted average commodity rates multiplied by the forecast kWh 
8 
commodity sales for each service class.  Second, commodity revenues 
9 
include the LTC, which is based on the net market value associated with 
10 
legacy purchase power contracts entered into before June 1, 2001.  Third, 
11 
commodity revenues include the NHA, which is the net market value 
12 
associated with purchase power contracts or financial hedges entered after 
13 
June 1, 2001.  Fourth, commodity revenues include the net market value 
14 
associated with NYPA Rural and Domestic power and the benefit of the 
15 
monthly Residential Consumer Discount Program payment.  The monthly 
16 
net market value of these contracts (i.e., the over/under Market Variable 
17 
Costs) is the contract costs less the projected market value of the generation, 
18 
as determined by the New York State Independent System Operator 
19 
(“NYISO”) zonal forward prices. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 17 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel

D. Other Components of Revenue Forecast 
1 
Q. 
How were the remaining components of the revenue forecast developed 
2 
– specifically for the MFC surcharge, System Benefit Charge (“SBC”), 
3 
and Dynamic Load Management (“DLM”) surcharge, and ESCO 
4 
commodity revenue? 
5 
A. 
These additional revenue components are separate surcharges that are 
6 
applicable to specific service classes as described in the Electric Tariff.  
7 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-2), Schedules 1-3 reflect the forecast of these 
8 
components based on the current surcharge rates applied to the sales 
9 
forecast for each service class.  The revenue forecast for the MFC surcharge, 
10 
which is designed to recover electric supply related costs, was developed by 
11 
applying the current MFC Uncollectible Expense and Working Capital 
12 
percentages to the forecast full service supply charges, and the Supply 
13 
Procurement and Credit and Collections charges to the Full Service kWh.  
14 
SBC recovers the cost of the New York State Energy Research and 
15 
Development Authority (“NYSERDA”) Clean Energy Fund budgeted to the 
16 
Company.  The DLM forecast is based on the reconciled Historic Test Year 
17 
amount increased by general inflation.  The calculations are shown in 
18 
Exhibit __ (RRP-3), Schedule 40.  The forecast ESCO commodity revenues 
19 
were developed by taking the total Company forecasted kWh usage by 
20 


--- Page 18 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 15 of 91 
service class and subtracting the full-service kWh, then multiplying by the 
1 
applicable forecasted $/kWh charge for that class each month. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
How did the Company forecast miscellaneous revenues? 
4 
A. 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-2), Schedule 4 sets out the forecast methodology for 
5 
each item included under miscellaneous revenues. 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
How was the forecast of Wholesale Transmission Revenue developed? 
8 
A. 
As explained in the direct testimony of the Revenue Requirements panel, 
9 
the Company is proposing to retain the FERC return on equity (“ROE”) for 
10 
the WNY Public Policy Transmission Needs (“PPTN”) projects.  This will 
11 
preserve the FERC ordered cost allocation that represents a beneficiary pay 
12 
principle where Company wholesale and retail transmission service 
13 
customers pay the same rate for the WNY PPTN project and no more or less 
14 
than what FERC deems just and reasonable.  Retaining the FERC ROE 
15 
ensures a level playing field for incumbent and non-incumbent transmission 
16 
developers competing in the NYISO Order 1000 process.  Therefore, the 
17 
WNY PPTN projects that are included in the forecast of “Wholesale 
18 
Transmission” revenue were calculated using the return on equity (“ROE”) 
19 
that is being proposed in this rate filing (“State ROE”), which allows the 
20 
Company to fully realize the FERC-approved ROE in the NYISO Open 
21 


--- Page 19 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 16 of 91 
Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”).  The calculation of the Wholesale 
1 
Transmission revenue is shown in Exhibit __ (E-RDP-2), Schedule 4, pages 
2 
1-7.    
3 
 
4 
The proposed Transmission Revenue Adjustment (“TRA”) targets would 
5 
typically match the forecast of Wholesale Transmission Revenue in the Rate 
6 
Year and Data Years, but as explained above, the Wholesale Transmission 
7 
Revenue will assume State ROE and the TRA targets will assume FERC 
8 
ROE for the WNY PPTN projects beginning in Data Year 1 when the 
9 
projects are expected to be in service.  Each month during the term of the 
10 
rate plan, the actual monthly transmission revenue (including FERC ROE 
11 
for the WNY PPTN projects beginning in Data Year 1 will be compared to 
12 
the TRA targets which will also reflect the FERC ROE for the WNY PPTN 
13 
projects.  The resulting over or under recoveries will be refunded to or 
14 
recovered from the Company’s retail customers.

16 
IV. 
Embedded Cost of Service Study 
17 
A. Purpose of ECOSS and Overview of Methodology 
18 
Q. 
Please describe what an ECOSS is and why it is presented. 
19 
A. 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion fairly a utility’s total revenue 
20 
requirement, including plant and other investments, operating expenses, 
21 


--- Page 20 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 17 of 91 
depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes served by the utility.  The 
1 
ECOSS computes the return on rate base at present rates for the future rate 
2 
year, as well as the revenue that would need to be collected in the Rate Year 
3 
from each class to produce the system average target rate of return on rate 
4 
base.  This information provides valuable guidance in revenue allocation, 
5 
and in the development of rates, to recover the utility’s overall revenue 
6 
requirement from all rate classes. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Please summarize the ECOSS methodology used. 
9 
A. 
In preparing the ECOSS, the Company used the same methodology as in 
10 
the 2012 Electric Rate Case and the 2017 Electric Rate Case.  Each element 
11 
of the Company’s total revenue requirement was analyzed and assigned to 
12 
or allocated among the rate classes.  The ECOSS was performed using a 
13 
proprietary model developed by HSG Group.  This model uses the 
14 
traditional three-step process: (1) functionalization; (2) classification; and 
15 
(3) class allocation: 
16 
• In functionalization, the Company’s cost elements (which include costs 
17 
and expenses, as well as the rate base components) are assigned or 
18 
allocated among each of the electric functions identified in Appendix A 
19 
to the Commission’s November 9, 2011 “Order Directing Filing of 
20 


--- Page 21 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 18 of 91 
Embedded Cost Studies” (“November 9 Order”) in Case 00-M-0504 
1 
(“Unbundling Cost Study Case”). 
2 
• In classification, each functionalized cost element is separated into one 
3 
or more of demand, commodity and customer cost components. 
4 
• In class allocation, each functionally classified cost element is assigned 
5 
or allocated among one or more of the Company’s rate classes. 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
What is the purpose of the functionalization step of the ECOSS? 
8 
A. 
The functionalization step is used to separate costs by the utility’s basic 
9 
service functions.  For purposes of the ECOSS for the Company’s electric 
10 
operations, these functions are identified as either regulated or competitive 
11 
as follows: 
12 
Regulated Functions 
13 
• Transmission – Bulk transmission system, designed to move power 
14 
from generation sources to the primary distribution system, operating at 
15 
voltages of 22 kV and up. 
16 
• Primary Distribution – Designed to move power from the transmission 
17 
system to the secondary distribution system and to customers’ premises; 
18 
includes substations as well as conductors operating at voltages of 2.2 
19 
kV up to 15 kV and related assets. 
20 


--- Page 22 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 19 of 91 
• Secondary Distribution – Designed to move power from the primary 
1 
distribution system to customers’ premises; includes service drops. 
2 
• Billing – Includes meters and other assets and activities related to 
3 
connecting customers to the system and distributing electricity to them, 
4 
as well as billing and collecting for the services provided (including 
5 
Competitive Meter Data, Competitive Meter Services, Competitive 
6 
Meter Ownership). 
7 
• Regulatory – Regulatory items in the revenue requirement. 
8 
Competitive Functions  
9 
• Competitive Supply 
10 
• Competitive Collections 
11 
• Competitive Billing  
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Did the Company make any changes to the competitive functions 
14 
identified in the 2017 Electric Rate Case? 
15 
A. 
Yes.  The Company is no longer including Competitive Meter Data, 
16 
Competitive Meter Services, or Competitive Meter Ownership in the 
17 
Company’s competitive function study in accordance with the 
18 
Commission’s “Order Terminating Meter Programs” issued February 8, 
19 
2019 in Cases 18-E-0595, 00-E-0165, and 94-E-0952. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 23 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 20 of 91 
Q. 
What is the purpose of the classification step of the ECOSS? 
1 
A. 
The Company’s transmission and distribution system is designed, operated, 
2 
and maintained to meet three primary objectives: 
3 
1. Connect customers to the distribution system; 
4 
2. Meet the peak requirements of each customer; and 
5 
3. Deliver power to customers. 
6 
Based on these objectives, each functionalized cost element is classified as 
7 
being one or more of customer-related, demand-related, or commodity-
8 
related, depending on which of the foregoing objectives it serves. 
9 
 
10 
Customer-related costs are incurred for assets that attach a customer to the 
11 
distribution system and to operate and maintain those assets, to meter the 
12 
customer’s usage, and to maintain customer accounts.  Customer-related 
13 
costs are primarily a function of the number of customers served, incurred 
14 
by the Company regardless of whether a particular customer uses any 
15 
electricity, and typically do not vary with usage or load profile.  Customer-
16 
related costs include capital and operating costs associated with the 
17 
customer portion of the primary and secondary distribution system, as well 
18 
as capital and operating costs for transformers, services, and meters.  They 
19 
also include the costs of metering, billing, customer service, and accounting 
20 
and collection activities.  Customer-related cost elements are allocated 
21 


--- Page 24 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 21 of 91 
among the classes based primarily on per-customer costs incurred (e.g., 
1 
services and meters) and on the number of customers served by a particular 
2 
activity. 
3 
 
4 
Demand, or capacity, related cost elements are associated with plant that is 
5 
designed, installed, and operated to meet peak customer demand.  Demand-
6 
related components include transmission system, the demand component of 
7 
distribution plant (including portions of poles, towers and fixtures, overhead 
8 
conductors, underground conduits and underground conductors), as well as 
9 
localized distribution facilities and dedicated facilities that are designed to 
10 
satisfy individual customer maximum demands.  Demand-related cost 
11 
elements are allocated among the classes based on class non-coincident 
12 
peak demands, or class contributions to system peak demand. 
13 
 
14 
Cost elements that generally vary with the kWh of electricity delivered to 
15 
customers are classified as commodity-related. 
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Please explain how assets and costs were assigned or allocated among 
18 
the functions. 
19 
A. 
In general, functionalization follows costs as recorded in the FERC Uniform 
20 
System of Accounts; however, some accounts are functionalized to more 
21 


--- Page 25 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 22 of 91 
than one function.  For example, Overhead Conductors and Devices 
1 
(Account 365) and Underground Conductors and Devices (Account 367) 
2 
were functionalized to both Primary Distribution and Secondary 
3 
Distribution based on a special study.  In this study, circuit miles of assets 
4 
were separated by voltage level, corresponding to Primary and Secondary 
5 
voltages, and costs were allocated based on the voltage level splits.  The 
6 
study is presented in Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-3), Schedule 9U.  Poles, Towers 
7 
and Fixtures (Account 364) were functionalized based on a similar study 
8 
using overhead conductor linear miles, also presented in Exhibit ___ (E-
9 
RDP-3), Schedule 9U.  Other assets were functionalized by direct 
10 
assignment based on the definition of the functions (e.g., Station Equipment 
11 
(Account 360) was assigned to Primary, and Services (Account 369) were 
12 
assigned to Secondary) or were allocated based on an appropriate allocator 
13 
(e.g., General Plant was allocated based on the labor content of the 
14 
accounts). 
15 
 
16 
Costs were directly assigned to a function whenever possible.  For example, 
17 
Transmission Plant and Transmission Operation and Maintenance 
18 
(“O&M”) costs were directly assigned to the Transmission function.  Costs 
19 
related directly to particular assets, such as Maintenance of Overhead Lines 
20 
(Account 593), were allocated in proportion to the assets.

Q. 
Do all costs fit neatly into one of the classifications in the ECOSS - 
5

(“Overhead Assets”), and Underground Conduits and Underground 
21 


--- Page 28 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 25 of 91 
Conductors (“Underground Assets”) are classified to both demand and 
1 
customer. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Please describe the process for determining the portions of Overhead 
4 
Assets and Underground Assets that are classified as customer-related 
5 
versus demand-related. 
6 
A. 
The demand / customer splits for Overhead Assets and Underground Assets 
7 
were based on a minimum system study, which is presented in Exhibit ___ 
8 
(E-RDP-3), Schedule 9W.  In the minimum system study, the cost of the 
9 
smallest capacity conductors that the utility would install (i.e., the minimum 
10 
system), is determined; this minimum system would fulfill the purpose of 
11 
connecting customers to the distribution system.  Then, the cost of the entire 
12 
system is determined.  For both the minimum system and the entire system, 
13 
costs are determined using the current costs for the assets installed, or 
14 
functionally equivalent assets if current costs are not available.  The cost of 
15 
the minimum system is expressed as a percentage of the cost of the entire 
16 
system.  The ratio of minimum system cost to entire system cost is the 
17 
Customer component of costs.  The Customer component is allocated 
18 
among the rate classes on a per-customer basis, because the cost of the 
19 
minimum system is largely determined by the length of the conductors, 
20 
which in turn is determined by the number of customers connected. 
21 


--- Page 29 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 26 of 91 
 
1 
Separate computations were made, and a separate customer component was 
2 
computed, for each of Primary Overhead, Secondary Overhead, Primary 
3 
Underground and Secondary Underground.  In each case, the procedure was 
4 
as follows: 
5 
1) Conductor types now in service were identified, including the 
6 
number of feet installed; 
7 
2) For each conductor type with recent purchase and installation 
8 
history, the current cost per foot was determined; 
9 
3) For conductor types with no recent history, an equivalent conductor 
10 
(from 1) above) was selected, and the cost per foot was assigned; 
11 
4) The minimum cost conductor was identified; 
12 
5) The cost of the minimum system was computed as total conductor 
13 
feet times cost per foot of minimum cost conductor (from 4); and 
14 
6) The cost of the entire system was computed as conductor feet for 
15 
each type times cost per foot for that type. 
16 
The minimum system ratios, computed by dividing item (5) by (6), were 
17 
Primary Overhead, 89.6 percent; Secondary Overhead, 98.4 percent; 
18 
Primary Underground, 54.4 percent; and Secondary Underground, 13.1 
19 
percent. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 30 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 27 of 91 
The customer-related components of Primary Overhead, Secondary 
1 
Overhead, Primary Underground, and Secondary Underground were 
2 
computed by multiplying the account balances by the above percentages.  
3 
The remainder of each account is the demand-related component. 
4 
 
5 
Distribution costs that are related to particular assets were classified in 
6 
proportion to those assets.  Other costs, such as Operation Supervision and 
7 
Engineering (Account 580), were classified based on the labor content of 
8 
expense accounts because the costs consist primarily of labor.

almost all customers in SC-1, SC-1C, and SC-2-No demand; that is, no 
16 
further investment in higher capacity conductors would be required.  
17 
Therefore, no demand-related costs for Overhead Assets or Underground 
18 
Assets were allocated to SC-1, SC-1C, and SC-2-Non demand.

Q. 
Please explain the allocation step of the ECOSS. 
14 
A. 
In the allocation phase of the ECOSS, the cost elements that have been 
15 
functionalized and classified are allocated among the service classes.  There 
16 
are two types of allocation factors (allocators): external allocators and 
17 
internal allocators.  External allocators are based on special studies derived 
18 
from data in the utility’s accounting and other records.  For example, the 
19 
number of customers in each rate class is an external allocator that was used 
20 
in the Company’s ECOSS to allocate some of the customer-classified costs.  
21 


--- Page 32 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 29 of 91 
Other examples of external allocators are class non-coincident peak demand 
1 
(“NCP”), class contributions to system peak (“1CP”), annual kWh 
2 
deliveries and historic bad debt experience. 
3 
 
4 
Internal allocators may be based on a combination of external allocators, 
5 
costs that are directly assigned, and/or other internal allocators.  For 
6 
example, the allocator for property insurance expense is based on plant 
7 
investment assigned to each service class.  Therefore, it is necessary to 
8 
compute plant investment by service class before property insurance costs 
9 
can be allocated among the classes.

Q. 
Please describe the Historic Cost of Service Study submitted by the 
1 
Panel. 
2 
A. 
In accordance with Section 3.10.2 of the Joint Proposal in the 2017 Electric 
3 
Rate Case, the Company prepared a Historic Cost of Service Study 
4 
(“HCOSS”), submitted as Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-12).  The HCOSS reflects 
5 
the allocation of rate base, costs, and revenue in the Historic Test Year.  
6 
These amounts (i) are not weather normalized, (ii) include non-recurring 
7

8

9

10 
requirement in the Company’s ECOSS had to be allocated on a different 
11 
basis.  The HCOSS also could not be used to compute the MFC components 
12 
for the Rate Year.  Finally, the HCOSS cannot be used to determine class 
13 
revenue deficiencies (or excess) at present rates, class target revenue 
14 
requirements, or whether the proposed revenue allocation moves classes 
15 
closer to cost of service.  Therefore, the Company did not use the HCOSS 
16 
in revenue allocation or rate design.

B. Revenue Allocation 
1 
Q. 
Please summarize the methodology used to develop the Company’s 
2 
revenue allocation shown on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 1. 
3 
A.       The proposed revenue allocation is intended to move the revenue produced 
4 
by each service class closer to its revenue requirement as determined in the 
5 
ECOSS.   In developing the Company’s proposed revenue allocation, the 
6 
Panel considered the costs to provide the type and quality of service 
7 
required by each service class as determined in the ECOSS, while 
8 
mitigating extreme impacts on service classes, a widely-accepted concept 
9 
known as “gradualism.” 
10 
 
11 
A revenue increase, excluding gross revenue tax, of $99.292 million is 
12 
required to produce the target rate of return (Exhibit ___ (E-RRP-4, 
13 
Schedule 3, lines 27-29).  After reflecting changes in MFC and other 
14 
revenue, an increase in delivery rates of $102.269 million is needed (lines 
15 
30-37).  The amount to be recovered in Delivery rates is $1,683.2 million 
16 
(Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 3, line 19); the class revenue targets sum 
17 
to this amount (Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 1, line 37). 
18 
 
19 
The Company established a tolerance band, representing returns from 75 to 
20 
125 percent of the overall system return at current rates, equal to returns of 
21 


--- Page 41 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 38 of 91 
3.91 to 6.52 percent.  The use of the tolerance band allows the Company to 
1 
rely on the ECOSS results as a guide to allocating the increased revenue 
2 
requirement fairly, while also promoting the goal of gradualism.  The 
3 
Company determined whether each class was within the tolerance band and 
4 
under the average, within and close to the average, within and over the 
5 
average, above the band or well above the band. 
6 
 
7 
All classes were within the tolerance band, except for SC-1C – Residential 
8 
TOU, which was considerably above the band.  An increase in revenue of 
9 
2.00 percent is proposed for SC-1C.  All other classes are proposed to 
10 
increase by 6.2327 percent, the amount needed to produce the overall 
11 
revenue target.   
12 
 
13 
Q. 
What returns on rate base does the proposed revenue allocation 
14 
produce? 
15 
A. 
The proposed revenue allocation produces returns ranging from 4.7 percent 
16 
to 7.3 percent (except for SC1C, which is 14.8 percent) with the system 
17 
target return of 6.33 percent (line 46), and reflects the results of the ECOSS.

C. Electric Tariff Rate Design 
2 
1. Purpose of Rate Design and Guiding Principles 
3 
Q. 
What is the purpose of rate design? 
4 
A. 
The purpose of rate design is to determine the rates that will produce the 
5 
target revenues for each rate class as determined in the revenue allocation 
6 
process.   
7 
 
8 
Q.  
What considerations were used in developing the Company’s proposed 
9 
rates? 
10 
A. 
The Company’s primary considerations in developing rates were to collect 
11 
the target revenue for each service class determined in the revenue 
12 
allocation process, and to provide appropriate price signals to customers to 
13 
reflect the effect of their usage on the overall system.  In addition, an ETIP 
14 
Adder and NYPA Credit were calculated to take into account that the 
15 
Company’s energy efficiency budget (Energy Efficiency Transition 
16 
Implementation Plan or “ETIP”) is incorporated into base delivery rates, yet 
17 
customers with NYPA deliveries are exempt from paying ETIP costs.   
18 
 
19 
Q.  
What is the ETIP Adder? 
20 
A.  
The ETIP Adder is the amount of the ETIP that was included in base 
21 


--- Page 43 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 40 of 91 
delivery rates but is then provided back to NYPA customers in the form of 
1 
a NYPA credit representing NYPA customers’ exemption from the 
2 
requirement to pay ETIP costs.  This amount is then recovered back from 
3 
all customers in base delivery rates through the inclusion of the ETIP Adder. 
4 
 
5 
Q.  
How were the NYPA Credit and ETIP Adder calculated and allocated 
6 
to the service classes? 
7 
A. 
The ETIP costs allocated to each demand service class is divided by the 
8 
total kW for each respective demand service class to derive a $/kW ETIP 
9 
rate that has been included in base delivery rates.  This $/kW rate is then the 
10 
NYPA credit that will be provided to NYPA customers on their NYPA kW 
11 
delivered usage in a separate surcharge on their bill.  The ETIP Adder is 
12 
then derived by calculating the ETIP that will be credited back to NYPA 
13 
customers and subtracting the ETIP that will be collected from EJP 
14 
customers qualifying load.  EJP customers are subject to ETIP but their 
15 
incremental load is not included in base delivery rates.  The ETIP that will 
16 
be credited back to NYPA customers is determined as the NYPA credit 
17 
multiplied by the NYPA forecasted KW for each service class to determine 
18 
the costs to be recovered back from each service class.  The ETIP that will 
19 
be collected from EJP customers is determined as the EJP forecasted kW 
20 
for demand classes and forecasted kWh for the SC-2 non-demand class 
21 


--- Page 44 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 41 of 91 
multiplied by the ETIP Adder for all customers.  This cost is divided by 
1 
each service class’ total kW, or kWh for the SC-2 non-demand class, and 
2 
collected back through base delivery rates.  The derivation of the NYPA 
3 
Credit and ETIP Adder is provided in Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 4B.

Q.

11

12 
A.  
Yes.  As discussed above, the SC-1 peak demand can be met with the 
13

14

15

16

17 
though cost is determined by number of customers not demand level).  
18

19 
recovered in the on-peak rate (line 27).

VI. 
Merchant Function Charge 
2 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s current MFC. 
3 
A. 
The MFC is a charge that is applied to full-service customers (i.e., those 
4 
receiving both delivery and commodity sales service from the Company) 
5 
and includes several components that are designed to recover costs 
6 
associated with commodity-related credit and collections services, 
7 
commodity-related uncollectible account expense, electric supply 
8 
procurement costs, and working capital for electric supply. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
How did the Company calculate the commodity-related credit and 
11 
collections component of the MFC? 
12 
A. 
The commodity-related credit and collections revenue requirement was 
13 
determined as part of the ECOSS and appears on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), 
14 
Schedule 2.  The amount in each FERC account related to commodity-
15 


--- Page 49 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 46 of 91 
related credit and collections was identified in a special study.  These costs 
1 
represent collection efforts for both full-service customers and ESCO 
2 
customers in the POR program.  The revenue requirement was then split 
3 
into non-demand, demand, and outdoor lighting using the forecast of 
4 
uncollectible commodity revenue for both full-service customers and 
5 
customers in the POR program.  The per kWh rate was developed by 
6 
dividing the commodity-related credit and collections revenue requirement 
7 
allocated to non-demand, demand, and outdoor lighting classes by the 
8 
associated forecast full-service and POR kWh in each customer group.  In 
9 
addition to recovering these costs through the MFC, the applicable per kWh 
10 
rate will be applied to POR kWhs and recovered through a discount of 
11 
receivables purchased by the Company from the ESCOs.  The credit and 
12 
collections rate per kWh is equal to $0.00011 for non-demand customers, 
13 
$0.00000 for demand customers, and $0.00001 for outdoor lighting 
14 
customers, as shown on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-7), Schedule 1.   
15 
  
16 
Q. 
How did the Company calculate the commodity-related uncollectible

18 
A. 
As set forth in Exhibit ___ (SSP-3) to the direct testimony of the Shared

20 
percent.  To develop individual rates for non-demand, demand, and outdoor

lighting, the Company began with the Historic Test Year revenue plus late

6

7 
percentage related to electric purchased power, the Company multiplied the

Q. 
How is the MFC determined for each customer? 
15 
A.

16

17

18

21

NHA) plus the electricity supply procured by the Company.  The

4

5

6

7 
 
8

12 
Q.

13 
lower percentage than the HID facility prices. 
14 
A. 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-8), Schedule 10 details the justification for a lower 
15 
facility price increase for LED facilities compared to the HID SC-1 and SC-
16 
2 facilities.  Current LED luminaire prices are closer to their full 
17 
replacement costs (58 percent) as compared to the HID lamp and luminaire 
18 
prices (41 percent).  If the overall facility price increase of 6.25 percent was 
19 
applied to all HID and LED facilities, the LED prices would move even 
20 
closer to their replacement costs.  Instead, the Company proposes to move 
21 


--- Page 60 ---

the LED and HID facilities an equal percentage from their current price 
1

3 
applied to all other HID facilities.  During rate design, the final HID facility 
4 
increase was 6.27 percent as compared to the LED increase of 3.27 percent.  
5 
This differential can be seen in the facility price increases in Exhibit ___ 
6 
(E-RDP-8), Schedules 2 and 3.

XI. 
Residential Electric Vehicle Smart Charging Plan  
7 
Q.   
Please describe the rates applicable to customers on the Company’s 
8 
proposed EV Smart Plan. 
9 
A.  
The Company’s EV Smart Plan is described in detail in the direct testimony 
10 
of the EV Panel.  Customers enrolled in the program will enroll in one of 
11 
two tiers of electric vehicle maximum usage, up to 225 kWh of off-peak 
12 
charging per month (“Tier 1”) or up to 325 kWh of off-peak charging per 
13 
month (“Tier 2”).  The electric vehicle usage will be measured by the 
14 
customer’s applicable charger’s onboard meter by on-peak and off-peak 
15 
usage periods.  The on-peak period is 7:00 am to 11:00 pm year round and 
16 
the off-peak period is 11:00 pm to 7:00 am year round.  The customer will 
17 
be charged a fixed monthly EV charge of $20.00 for Tier 1 customers and 
18 
$25.00 for Tier 2 customers.  The fixed monthly EV charge is intended to 
19 
cover the customer’s off-peak EV kWh usage up to the Tier kWh level.  The 
20 
customer will be charged an EV On-peak charge of $0.13715/kWh for any 
21 


--- Page 64 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 61 of 91 
EV kWh usage during the on-peak period.  Any off-peak EV kWh usage 
1 
above the Tier usage level will be charged at the customer’s otherwise 
2 
applicable SC-1 charges, including surcharges each billing period.   
3 
 
4 
Q.   
How did the Company develop the fixed monthly EV charge? 
5 
A.  
The Company’s proposed fixed monthly EV charge includes i) an 
6 
incremental customer charge, ii) an EV off-peak delivery rate, and iii) an 
7 
EV off-peak supply rate.  The development of the incremental customer 
8 
charge of $8.00 per month is described in more detail in the direct testimony 
9 
of the Electric Vehicles Panel and shown in Exhibit __ (EVP-9).  The EV 
10 
off-peak delivery rate is based on the Company’s SC 1 VTOU off-peak 
11 
delivery rate and an estimate of the Company’s Systems Benefits Charge 
12 
$/kWh rate for the rate year.  The EV off-peak supply rate is based on i) 
13 
estimated annual off-peak forecasted supply rates, averaged for the 
14 
Company’s central, eastern and western regions, ii) a forecast of Clean 
15 
Energy Standard Supply surcharge rates, and iii) an estimate of MFC rates.  
16 
The fixed monthly EV Charge would be updated for subsequent rate years.  
17 
The detail on the rates used to develop the fixed monthly EV Charge is 
18 
provided in Exhibit __ (E-RDP-11), Schedule 1.  
19

B. Paperless Billing Credit 
15 
Q. 
Is the Company updating its paperless billing credit? 
16 
A. 
Yes.  The Company has updated the calculation of the paperless billing 
17 
credit.  This calculation is detailed in Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-6), Schedule 2, 
18 
page 1.  The credit is based on Historic Test Year costs adjusted for inflation 
19 
and represents the difference in cost to produce a paper bill versus 
20 
producing an electronic bill.  The paperless billing credit consists primarily 
21 


--- Page 71 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 68 of 91 
of the cost of paper, postage, and envelopes offset by electronic billing 
1 
costs. The Company’s forecast costs for the paperless billing credit yields a 
2 
change in the credit from the current $0.41 to $0.40.   
3 
 
4 
Q. 
Why does the Company make a normalizing adjustment to the Historic 
5 
Test Year Revenue Requirement to add back the cost for paperless 
6 
savings?  
7 
A. 
To properly provide credits in the Rate Year to existing electronically billed 
8 
customers (those customers who elected to receive electronic bills during 
9 
the Historic Test Year), an adjustment to the Historic Test Year is required 
10 
to add back the avoided cost of issuing a paper bill to those customers so 
11 
that the revenue requirement assumes all customers receive a paper bill.  
12 
This aligns the revenue requirements such that the paperless billing credit 
13 
then passes back an equal and offsetting credit to electronically billed 
14 
customers in the Rate Year. 
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Why does the Company believe this is an appropriate adjustment to 
17 
make? 
18 
A. 
The Paperless Billing Program is intended to be cost and revenue neutral. 
19 
Savings achieved by the Company (i.e., the cost of envelopes, paper, 
20 
postage, and processing, less the cost to provide an electronic bill), would 
21 


--- Page 72 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 69 of 91 
be returned to electronically billed customers in the form of a credit on each 
1 
bill. 
2

XIII. 
Marginal Cost of Service Study   
5 
Q. 
Please provide an overview of the Electric MCS. 
6 
A. 
The purpose of the MCS, presented in Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), is to 
7 
compute the incremental, or marginal, cost to the utility to provide the next 
8 
unit of service, i.e., the next kW of demand peak demand or the next 
9 
customer connected.  The results of the MCS are useful as a guide in rate 
10 
design. 
11 
 
12 
Q. 
How does an MCS differ from an ECOSS? 
13 
A. 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to allocate all of the utility’s costs.  MCS focus 
14 
on the change in costs associated with a change in output.  MCS are forward 
15 
looking and require estimates of future costs.  In addition, the costs included 
16 
in embedded cost studies may be lumpy because the utility’s capacity 
17 
additions may include more capacity than immediately needed, while 
18 
marginal costs are assumed to be incurred only to meet future needs. 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 89 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 86 of 91 
Q. 
Please specify the components of marginal costs in the MCS. 
1 
A. 
The MCS estimates the cost of providing an additional unit of service.  In 
2 
this case, service includes two components: 
3 
• Marginal demand-related costs: The initial capital cost needed to 
4 
provide an additional unit of peak demand, plus the direct O&M costs 
5 
related to the assets, and related costs for A&G, general plant, insurance 
6 
and property taxes.  The assets included are: 
7 
o Transmission/Subtransmission plant 
8 
o Primary/Secondary Plant, comprising Poles, Towers and 
9 
Fixtures; Overhead Conductors; Underground Conductors and 
10 
Underground Conduits 
11 
o Transformers 
12 
• Marginal customer-related costs:  The initial capital costs needed to 
13 
attach an additional customer to the system, plus the direct O&M costs 
14 
related to the assets, and annual costs for customer-related activities 
15 
such as metering, billing and customer support.  The assets included are 
16 
Services and Meters. 
17 
 
18 
In each case, the initial capital costs are converted to an annual cost, 
19 
representing the amount that would be included in the annual revenue 
20 
requirement to reflect return on rate base plus associated income tax, 
21 


--- Page 90 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 87 of 91 
depreciation expense, property tax, insurance and related costs for 
1 
administrative and general activities and general plant.  The annual revenue 
2 
requirement needed for one dollar of initial capital (Economic Carrying 
3 
Charge Rate or “ECCR”) for each asset type in this MCS is presented on 
4 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10) Schedule 5, with supporting information in 
5 
Schedules 5A, 5B and 5C. 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
What rate classes were included in the MCS? 
8 
A. 
The MCS used the same rate classes as the ECOSS discussed above. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
Please describe how the marginal demand-related cost was calculated. 
11 
A. 
The marginal demand-related cost reflects the Company’s projected capital 
12 
costs to serve additional demand, and the additional demand that can be 
13 
served.  The demand-related costs are stated in capital dollars per additional 
14 
kW served, and are based on the Company’s planned additions (for 
15 
Transmission/Subtransmission), recent additions (for Primary/Secondary) 
16 
and current costs (for Transformers).  These costs were inflated from 2016 
17 
dollars to 2018 dollars.  The capital costs are presented on Exhibit ___ (E-
18 
RDP-10) Schedules 6, 6A, 6B and 6C. 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 91 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 88 of 91 
The capital cost was converted to an annual revenue requirement reflecting 
1 
return on rate base plus associated income tax, depreciation expense, 
2 
property tax, insurance and related costs for administrative and general 
3 
activities and general plant, plus direct annual O&M costs for the assets, 
4 
using the ECCRs presented on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10) Schedule 5.  The 
5 
annual demand-related costs are presented on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), 
6 
Schedule 2. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Please describe how the marginal customer-related cost was calculated. 
9 
A. 
The marginal customer-related cost reflects the Company’s projected 
10 
capital costs for services and meters to serve new customers.  These costs 
11 
are computed in the ECOSS and are presented on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), 
12 
Schedules 6, 6D and 6E. 
13 
 
14 
The capital costs were converted to annual revenue requirements reflecting 
15 
return on rate base plus associated income tax, depreciation expense, 
16 
property tax, insurance and related costs for administrative and general 
17 
activities and general plant, plus direct annual O&M costs for the assets, 
18 
using the ECCRs presented on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), Schedule 5.  In 
19 
addition, annual costs were added for customer-related activities such as 
20 
metering, billing and customer support, as presented on Exhibit ___ (E-
21 


--- Page 92 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 89 of 91 
RDP-10), Schedule 4.  The annual customer-related costs are presented on 
1 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), Schedule 3. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Did the Panel calculate a marginal revenue requirement? 
4 
A. 
Yes.  The marginal revenue requirement is the marginal demand-related 
5 
cost multiplied by peak demand for each rate class, plus the marginal 
6 
customer-related cost times the number of customers.  The calculations are 
7 
presented on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), Schedule 1. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Were the results of the MCS used to design delivery rates? 
10 
A. 
Yes, the MCS results were used to develop the EZR and EJP rates the 
11 
Company proposed in its filing.   
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please describe how the EZR and EJP rates were developed. 
14 
A. 
To determine the marginal rates for EZR and EJP customers, the Company 
15 
set a revenue target by service class and voltage delivery level equal to the 
16 
sum of the marginal demand costs and the marginal customers costs derived 
17 
in the Company’s MCS shown in Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), Schedule 7.  
18 
From the sum of these costs, the Company subtracted the customer charge 
19 
revenue at proposed rates by service classification and voltage delivery 
20 
level.  The remaining costs were then divided by the forecast kWh and kW 
21 


--- Page 93 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 90 of 91 
billing determinants to arrive at the marginal rates applicable to EZR and 
1 
EJP customers certified after February 1, 2011.  For EJP rates, the ETIP 
2 
Adder for all customers, which is derived in Schedule 4B of Exhibit___(E-
3 
RDP-4) is added to the marginal rates to determine the final EJP rates. The 
4 
calculations and the resulting rates for both EJP and EZR can be found on 
5 
Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), Schedule 7, page 1.  However, these rates would 
6 
represent a significant increase to the EJP and EZR service classes, with the 
7 
exception of SC2 non-demand, when compared to the Rate Year 4 
8 
(FY2022) rates that will be in effect just prior to the start of the Rate Year 
9 
(July 1, 2021) of the proposed rate plan.  Therefore, the Company proposes 
10 
to phase-in the increases compared to Rate Year 4 EZR and EJP rates over 
11 
five years to mitigate the bill impacts on these customers and continue to 
12 
provide a discount from the proposed standard tariff rates.  The Company’s 
13 
proposed five-year phase-in rates are provided in Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-10), 
14 
Schedule 8, Page 1 for EJP and Page 2 for EZR.  The Company may re-
15 
evaluate the phase-in of these rates depending on the final revenue 
16 
requirement in this case.  
17 
 
18 


--- Page 94 ---
Testimony of the Electric Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 91 of 91 
Q. 
Why is the ETIP Adder for all customers added to the EJP marginal 
1 
cost rates to determine the final EJP rates? 
2 
A. 
EZR customers are currently exempt from paying SBC and ETIP while EJP 
3 
customers are not exempt.  EJP qualifying usage which is considered to be 
4 
incremental usage is not subject to base delivery rates which already include 
5 
ETIP costs.  Therefore, the Company is proposing to add ETIP costs to the 
6 
EJP marginal cost rates to ensure they are paying their share of ETIP costs. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Does this conclude your testimony? 
9 
A. 
Yes, it does.  
10

Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The testimony of the Rate Design Panel describes the purpose of performing an Embedded Cost 
of Service Study (“ECOSS”), and summarizes the methodology used to prepare the ECOSS in 
this proceeding of Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) (“NiMo-Electric” or the 
“Company”).  The testimony describes the three-step ECOSS process (functionalization, 
classification, class allocation) used to analyze each element of the revenue requirement, in order 
to assign or allocate it among the rate classes. 
This Schedule 10 describes the ECOSS methodology in more detail.  Part 1 describes the three-
step ECOSS process. 
Part 2 describes how each element of the revenue requirement (rate base, expense and revenue) 
was assigned or allocated in each of the three steps.  Rate base, expenses and revenues are 
identified using the Uniform System of Accounts (FERC Accounts).  Part 2 serves as a guide 
when reviewing the other schedules in this exhibit. 
Part 1. DETAILED ECOSS METHODOLOGY 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion fairly a utility’s total revenue requirement, including 
plant and other investments, operating expenses, depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes 
served by the utility.  The ECOSS computes for each rate class the revenue to be collected to 
produce the overall required rate of return on rate base.  This information provides valuable 
guidance in revenue allocation, and in the development of rates, to recover the revenue 
requirement from all rate classes. 
The three steps of the ECOSS are: 
Functionalization-  Cost elements are separated among the utility’s basic service 
functions, by determining what physical purpose each cost element serves.  The 
Company’s functions are: Transmission; Primary Distribution; Secondary Distribution; 
Billing; Regulatory; Competitive Supply; Competitive Collections; Competitive Billing; 
Competitive Meter Data; Competitive Meter Services; and Competitive Meter 
Ownership. 
Classification-  Each functionalized cost element is classified as Customer-related 
(connect customers to the distribution system); Demand-related (meet peak capacity 
requirements) or Commodity-related (deliver energy to customers). 
Class Allocation-  Cost elements that have been functionalized and classified are 
allocated among the service classes, using an appropriate allocation factor for each cost 


--- Page 302 ---
Exhibit___ (E-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 2 of 6 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
element.  Allocation factors can be external (e.g., number of customers, kWh delivered, 
class peak requirements, class contribution to system peak, and historical bad debt 
experience) or internal (e.g., property insurance is based on plant investment). 
Part 2. ALLOCATOR FOR EACH ELEMENT OF THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT 
A. Rate Base 
1. Intangible Plant (Account 302) 
Primarily the cost of franchises and other rights.  Allocated in proportion to plant 
investment. 
2. Transmission Plant (Account 350-359) 
The bulk transmission system moves power from generation sources to the primary 
distribution system, and is designed to meet system peak requirements.  It operates at 
voltages of 22 kV and up.  Classified as Demand and allocated among the rate classes 
based on contribution to the system peak (“1CP”). 
3. Primary Distribution and Secondary Distribution Plant (FERC Accounts 360-374) 
Land & Land Rights; Structures and Improvements; Station Equipment –This plant 
connects the Transmission system to the Primary Distribution system, and is designed 
to meet system peak requirements at Primary voltages.  Classified as Demand and 
allocated among the rate classes based on class non-coincident peak requirements at 
Primary voltages (“NCP-Pri”). 
Poles, Towers and Fixtures; Overhead Conductors; Underground Conductors; and 
Underground Conduits- This includes: 
Primary Distribution plant, which moves power from the transmission system to 
the secondary distribution system and to customers’ premises; operates at voltages 
of 2.2 kV up to 15 kV and related assets; and 
Secondary Distribution plant, which moves power from the primary distribution 
system to customers’ premises; includes service drops. 
These plant assets are separated between Primary and Secondary based on the voltages 
at which they operate. 
Design considerations for Primary Distribution and Secondary Distribution plant 
include extending the system to serve customers (i.e., customer-related) and providing 


--- Page 303 ---
Exhibit___ (E-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 3 of 6 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
capacity to meet local peak customer requirements (i.e., demand-related).  Therefore 
the cost of this plant is classified as partly customer-related and partly demand-related. 
A minimum system study was performed to determine the customer-related portion, 
representing the cost of extending the system to customers.  The study and the results 
are described in the testimony of the Rate Design Panel. 
The balance, the demand component, was allocated among the classes based on class 
non-coincident design-day requirements (“NCP”).  The NCPs were developed by 
computing the load factor for each rate class and applying it to forecast kWh. 
However, the conductors identified in the minimum system study have load-carrying 
capacity, even though their cost is determined primarily by length.  In fact, the 
minimum system would be able to meet the peak load for all or almost all customers in 
SC-1, SC-1C, and SC-2-No demand; that is, no further investment in higher capacity 
conductors would be required.  Therefore, no demand-related costs for Overhead 
Assets or Underground Assets were allocated to SC-1, SC-1C, and SC-2-No demand. 
Transformers – Transformers are sized to meet the peak needs of local customers.  A 
special study identified, for each transformer on the system, the customers served, by 
rate class.  The cost of each transformer (using current cost) was allocated based on the 
estimated NCP per customer of the customers served. 
Services- Services connect the customer to the Primary or Secondary Distribution 
plant.  There is a direct correspondence between number of customers and number of 
services; therefore, services are classified as customer-related.  The costs are estimated 
based on the current cost for a typical service line for each rate class, which reflects the 
peak requirements for each rate class. 
Meters- Meters (including installation costs and house regulators) are classified as 
customer-related, and allocated based on the current cost for a typical meter for each 
rate class. 
4. General Plant (Accounts 389-399) 
Primarily Structures & improvements; Tools, shop & garage; and office furniture and 
equipment.  General plant was functionalized, classified and class allocated in 
proportion to the direct labor content of operating and maintenance expense, because 
these assets primarily support direct labor. 
5. Depreciation Reserve (Accounts 108 and 111) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 


--- Page 304 ---
Exhibit___ (E-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 4 of 6 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
6. Other Rate Base Items 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
Materials & Supplies, Prepayments and Cash Working Capital (non-commodity) were 
allocated in proportion to O&M costs.  Accumulated Deferred Income Tax and CWIP 
were allocated in proportion to plant in service.  Regulatory Assets and Earnings Base 
Adjustment were allocated in proportion to rate base.  Cash Working Capital 
(commodity) was allocated in proportion to Commodity revenue. 
B. Expenses 
1. Purchased Power (Account 555)- Allocated in proportion to  
2. Transmission O&M (Account 580)- Allocated based on 1CP (same as Transmission 
plant). 
3. Distribution O&M (Accounts 580-599)- Most accounts were allocated on the same 
basis as the asset to which the account relates.  Operations Supervision & Engineering 
(Account 580) and Operations Supervision & Engineering- (Account 590) were 
allocated based on direct labor content of O&M accounts.  Miscellaneous Expenses 
(Account 588) Allocated based on a special study to identify the activities in the 
account.  Load Dispatching (Account 581) was allocated based on kWh deliveries 
because this activity takes place year round (actually minute-by-minute). 
4. Customer Accounts Expenses (FERC Accounts 901-919) 
These accounts were functionalized among the following functions based on a study of 
competitive functions performed by the utility: Billing; Competitive Supply; 
Competitive Collections; Competitive Billing.  The accounts are all customer-related. 
Supervision (Account 901)-  Allocated in proportion to Customer records and 
collections (Account 903) 
Meter reading (Account 902)-  Allocated based on current cost of meters. 
Customer records and collections (Account 903)-  Billing-related activities are Print 
and mail bills and a portion of Call Center (related to Billing inquiries).  Collections-
related activities are a portion of Call center and a portion of Credit & collections.  
Distribution-related activities are the balance of Call center, the balance of Credit & 
collections, Field Collections, Print & Mail, Account Maintenance and Payment 
Processing.

Exhibit___ (E-RDP-3)

Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Each functionalized activity was allocated among the rate classes using an appropriate 
allocation factor, and the results were summed to compute allocators for Account 903- 
Distribution, Account 903- Billing and Account 903- Collections. 
Uncollectible accounts expense (Account 904)-  Allocated based on historical write-off 
experience. 
Miscellaneous customer accounts (Account 905)-  Activities support customer contact; 
allocated in proportion to Account 903. 
Customer assistance expenses (Account 908)-  This account includes several programs, 
which were brohen out and allocated as follows- Discounts offered to low income 
customers and economic development discounts, (allocated based on the Company’s 
overall revenue requirement); costs recovered in the SBC charge (allocated based on 
the SBC revenue); ETIP costs (allocated based on the programs involved).  The 
balance of costs were allocated based on a special study, presented on Exhibit___(E-
RDP-3, Schedule 9Q). 
Customer assistance expenses (Account 910), Demonstration & selling (Account 912) 
and Advertising (Account 913)- Allocated based on number of customers. 
5. Administrative & General expenses (FERC Accounts 920-939) are grouped as follows: 
 Most A&G expenses are labor-related, and are functionalized, classified and 
allocated in proportion to direct labor content of O&M accounts 
 Plant-related expenses are functionalized, classified and allocated in proportion 
to according to gross plant 
 Regulatory commission expense (Account 928) was allocated based on Rate 
base 
 A portion of A&G Salaries (Account 920) related to major accounts was 
allocated to the appropriate classes on a per-customer basis. 
 Street Lighting programs were directly assigned. 
 Account 931, representing costs from the ServiceCo, and including IT-related 
costs, was allocated based on a study of the projects included. 
6. Depreciation and Amortization Expense (FERC Accounts 403-407) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
7. Taxes other than on income

Exhibit___ (E-RDP-3)

Page 6 of 6 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Electric) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Property taxes were allocated in proportion to plant, excluding services and meters.  
Payroll taxes were allocated in proportion to direct labor content.  Other taxes were 
allocated in proportion to plant. 
8. Income Tax Expense 
Income Tax Expense at present rates was allocated in proportion to Pretax income at 
present rates.  Income Tax Expense at the revenue requirement (i.e., proposed rates) 
was computed based on the target return used to develop the revenue requirement. 
C. Revenue 
Revenue from base delivery (including transmission) charges, commodity, MFC and 
SBC were assigned based on forecast revenue at present rates. 
Wholesale Transmission Revenue was allocated in the same manner as Transmission 
assets (1CP).  Late payment revenue was allocated based on historical write-off 
experience.  Pole attachment revenue was allocated in the same manner as the assets 
that support the revenue.  Revenue representing recovery of certain costs (supervision 
of field construction and direct load control) were allocated in proportion to the O&M 
accounts where the costs are reflected.  CSS Reestablishment revenue was allocated 
based on number of customers.  Special L Meter revenue was directly assigned to the 
appropriate classes.  Other revenue was allocated based on the Company’s overall 
revenue requirement.

Professional Experience  
Director, NY Pricing, Jun 2019 – Present 
I am responsible for the oversight of the study, analysis, and design of delivery service rates, rate 
contracts, surcharge adjustment factors, riders and terms and condition of service for National Grid 
USA’s three New York State gas utilities, including KEDNY, KEDLI, and Niagara Mohawk Power 
Corporation, and for Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation’s electric utility. 
Manager, NY Gas Pricing, Dec 2015 – Jun 2019  
My responsibilities included the supervision of the study, analysis and design of retail gas delivery 
service rates and terms and conditions for gas service, including testifying and supporting such rates and 
tariffs before the NYPSC for National Grid USA’s three New York State gas utilities – KEDNY, 
KEDLI and Niagara Mohawk. The gas pricing department is also responsible for providing customer 
service and billing support, negotiated contract support, and guidance in the interpretation and 
application of retail gas delivery service tariffs.  
Senior/Lead Pricing Analyst, NY Electric Pricing-National Grid, Jan 2006 – Dec 2015  
My responsibilities as lead analyst included analytical support for electric standby service including cost 
and regulatory analysis, deferral accounting process design, rate design, and discovery responses.  I also 
had responsibility for the development of various surcharge factors including the monthly and annual 
reconciliations for the Company’s electric commodity reconciliations and merchant function charges.  I 
was also the regulatory lead for several new initiatives including the development of residential time of 
use rates and the implementation of the NYPA residential agricultural discount program.  
Senior Financial Analyst, Planning and Financial Analysis- National Grid Feb 2000 – Jan 2006  
My responsibilities as senior analyst included the preparation of margin reports monthly for internal 
management review, the evaluation of margin variances, the preparation of monthly revenue analysis and 
development of the annual budget for margin related items.

Professional Experience 
 
Manager, NY Electric Pricing, National Grid, May, 2014 - Present 
My responsibilities as a manager includes the supervision of the study, analysis and design of National 
Grid’s upstate New York retail electric delivery service rates, rate contracts, surcharge adjustment factor 
clauses, riders, and terms and conditions for electric service, including developing tariffs and testimony 
supporting such rates before the NYPSC.  Other duties performed by Electric Pricing include the 
preparation of the electric revenue forecast, sales data and analyses, as well as providing customer billing 
support and guidance in the interpretation and application of retail delivery service tariffs.   
 
Manager, Billing Project Management Services, National Grid, October 2011 – May 2014 
My responsibilities included the support and operations of customer billing for all National Grid 
companies and LIPA.  This included overseeing all billing projects necessary to facilitate regulatory 
changes to customer retail bills, and ensuring regulatory price changes are implemented accurately and on 
time in three customer billing systems.  I was also responsible for daily billing operations management as 
well as ensuring successful outcomes on SOX and Price Waterhouse billing audits. 
 
Manager, Load Research & Analysis, National Grid,  March 2008 - October 2011 
My responsibilities included managing a team in the preparation of load research studies to support 
electric rate cases, customer retail billing, settlement, and special studies for all National Grid companies 
and LIPA. Responsibilities also included overseeing survey meter design sample studies for all 
companies and ensuring a sufficient sample of survey meters in the field to support load studies.  Other 
duties included managing the administration of the Company’s Energy Profiler Online service and 
preparation of the development and publication of the LIPA annual population survey report. 
 
Transmission Account Manager, Transmission Commercial Services, National Grid, October 2005 – 
March 2008 
My responsibilities included managing the Company’s interconnection process in compliance with FERC 
policies and orders, and acting as primary contact for wholesale generators interconnecting to National 
Grid’s transmission system in both New York and New England. I developed and managed the 
Company’s interconnection agreements and contracts for studies and services for over fifty generators 
and municipalities.   
 
Senior/Principal Analyst, Electric Pricing, National Grid, February 2002 – October 2005 
My responsibilities included developing and administrating Niagara Mohawk’s flexible retail electric 
contracts for large commercial and industrial customers.  This included developing innovative pricing 
options and proposals for electric customers with competitive alternatives.  I was also responsible for 
developing the budget forecast for electric revenue and deferral discounts for flexible rate contracts and 
standby service customers.

Power Contract Specialist, Customer Contract Services, Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation, September 
1997 – February 2002 
My responsibilities included designing pricing proposals and contracts for electric customers.  I assisted 
in the design of Service Classification No. 12, flexible rate discount program. I worked on the 
implementation of the PowerChoice Program and the implementation of a transition plan for Service 
Classification No. 12 Optional Transition contract customers. I also contributed to the development of 
Niagara Mohawk’s Emergency Demand Response and Day Ahead Demand Response Programs.  
 
Power Contract Specialist, Transmission Scheduling, Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation, April 1997 – 
September 1997 
My responsibilities included the daily scheduling of Niagara Mohawk’s power purchases and sales, and 
electric wheeling arrangements through the New York Power Pool. I also developed Niagara Mohawk’s 
daily electric load forecast for use in daily scheduling of generation, power sales and purchases. 
 
Power Contract Specialist, Unregulated Generation, Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation,  May 1993 –   
April 1997 
My responsibilities included developing and negotiating power purchase agreements and contract buyout 
agreements with independent power producers to reduce the Company’s liability related to over market 
priced power supply contracts. 
 
Leadership Development Experience Associate, Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation, May 1992 – May 
1993 
I participated in a program to develop leadership qualities and expand my understanding of the utility 
industry and internal company organizations as preparation for future roles.  This included a temporary 
six month assignment in the Unregulated Generation department. 
 
Assistant/Junior Engineer, Instrumentation & Control Design, Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation, June 
1989 – May 1992 
My responsibilities included acting as project engineer for the design and installation of control and 
instrumentation systems at Niagara Mohawk’s fossil generating stations, both individually and under the 
supervision of a more senior engineer.
